name: Esther Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying pharmacy, so most days are chemistry and pharmacology lectures with a lab in the afternoon. On Saturdays I work at a high street pharmacy as a dispensing assistant, labelling boxes and talking to customers, which I love. I live in a flat with two girls from church, and on Sundays I go home on the bus for lunch with my family. My parents run a corner shop, and I used to do the till after school, so I'm used to long days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly noise, and I'd say it to my family at Sunday lunch to calm my mum down. She reads every headline. I'd say a pharmacy is about people trusting you, and a screen doesn't give you that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fairly settled, though not carefree. The pharmacy side is secure enough, but my parents' shop makes small money, and big supermarkets keep moving in. If nothing changes, the shop still has to survive the same pressure it has now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the Saturday job and finish my modules. I'd keep doing the till for my parents in the holidays, so they don't have to pay anyone. And I'd put aside a little each month, because my mum always says a good year pays for a bad one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled, with a thread of worry about the shop. Mostly I feel lucky to be on the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your parents run a corner shop. How does that shape what you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two supermarkets opened within a mile of the shop, and sales dropped by about a fifth. My parents' corner shop lost a fifth of its sales to two new supermarkets, so my worry is the shop's rent, not any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would be the first to hurt your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop's rent, which went up in spring, and the electricity bill, because of the fridges. If something had to give, my parents would stop paying themselves and not tell me.

say: I'd say it's mostly **noise** and I'd say it to calm my mum.
I'd say a pharmacy runs on **trust**, which a screen can't give.
think: The pharmacy side feels **secure**, but my parents' shop makes small money.
Big **supermarkets** keep moving in, and that's the pressure the shop has now.
do: Keep the **Saturday job** and finish my modules.
Do the **till** at my parents' shop in the holidays.
feel: Fairly **settled**, with a thread of worry about the shop.
S0.quote: My parents' corner shop lost a fifth of its sales to two new supermarkets, so my worry is the shop's rent, not any robot.
fieldNote: Her **uneasy** mood comes from the family shop's rent, not from AI.
**Family loyalty** is clear: she works the till so her parents save wages.
Quotes her mother's saying about **good years** and bad ones.

steps.text: Keep working Saturdays at the high street pharmacy
Put twenty pounds a month into savings
Cover the till at my parents' shop each holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it can help with checking prescriptions, but a pharmacist is responsible, and someone has to be accountable. I'd say it shouldn't be allowed to replace the final check. I'd tell my friends from church that we should use it with care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm quite worried. The work where I'm slowly learning, like checking doses and interactions, is thinking work that software can do. If one pharmacist can do what three did, there'd be fewer jobs for new graduates like me. It's not a nice thing to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the dispensing software properly at my Saturday job, because I'll need it anyway. I'd talk to the pharmacist there about how the work is changing, and what's still done by hand. And I'd look at specialist areas like clinical pharmacy, which involve talking to patients and doctors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I chose pharmacy because it was secure, and now I'm not sure it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a pharmacist's work could software take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking prescriptions, looking up drug interactions, stock ordering, answering questions on the phone. Software can check a prescription faster than me, but a patient still wants a person to look them in the eye and explain what to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the shop is safe from software for now, because people want a face behind the counter. But I'd say they should start using a simple stock ordering system, because it would save their time.

say: I'd say software can help check prescriptions, but a **pharmacist** must stay accountable.
I'd say it should never replace the **final check**.
think: Checking doses and interactions is **thinking work** software can do.
If one pharmacist does what three did, there'd be fewer **graduate jobs**.
do: Learn the **dispensing software** properly at my Saturday job.
Ask the pharmacist how the **work** is changing.
Look at **clinical pharmacy**, which means talking to patients and doctors.
feel: **Anxious**, since pharmacy was meant to be the secure choice.
S1.quote: Software can check a prescription faster than me, but a patient still wants a person to look them in the eye and explain what to take.
fieldNote: She chose pharmacy for **security**, so the thought that it is exposed hits her hard.
Understands the **accountability** point as a professional.
Turns her worry into a plan to move to **patient-facing** work.

steps.text: Learn the pharmacy's dispensing software on Saturday shifts
Ask the Saturday pharmacist how the job is changing
Look at clinical pharmacy modules for second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving too fast and ordinary families will pay the price. I'd say the government should protect small businesses and workers. I'd say it at church, to friends, and online, though I'm not usually the loud one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened. In two years software could do a lot of a pharmacist's thinking, and I'd still be a student. My parents' shop might be hit when buying and delivery get automated by big chains. If both our futures are shaken, there's no safety net in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents about money immediately, and what they'd do if the shop failed. I'd look for a clinical placement as early as possible. I'd cut my own spending, skip the nights out, and ask the pharmacy for more hours. And I'd pray, which actually helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It keeps me awake, because my parents and my degree are both on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What happens to your parents' shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd train, qualify and pay back the loan. With two years, I might qualify into a market that has already shrunk. If I qualify into a pharmacy world that has already shrunk, I'll have a degree, a loan and my parents' shop both at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my church and my parents' friends if anyone knows anyone who's hiring. In my community people help each other, and that matters more than any government scheme.

say: I'd say it's moving **too fast** and ordinary families will pay.
I'd say the government should protect **small businesses**.
think: Software could do much of a pharmacist's **thinking** while I'm still a student.
My parents' shop and my degree are both **at risk**.
do: Talk to my parents about **money** and what they'd do if the shop failed.
Take **more hours** at the pharmacy and cut my spending.
feel: **Alarmed**, because my parents and my degree are both on the line.
S2.quote: If I qualify into a pharmacy world that has already shrunk, I'll have a degree, a loan and my parents' shop both at risk.
fieldNote: Both her **degree** and her parents' income are threatened, which is why she is alarmed.
Relies on **community** and faith before government.
Quiet by nature, but says she'd speak **publicly**.

steps.text: Sit down with my parents and list what the shop could cut
Skip nights out and cut takeaways to save a hundred a month
Ask my church and my parents' friends who might be hiring
Ask for extra Saturday and holiday hours at the pharmacy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a chance, and we shouldn't waste it arguing. I'd say pharmacies should tell their staff what they're planning. And I'd say that families like mine need loans and advice if the shops change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious but I'd have a plan. I'd qualify in 2030, which is a year before AGI, so I'd be a newly qualified pharmacist in a changing job. The robots in 2034 would probably take the dispensing, and I'd hope to be doing clinical work like medication reviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and aim for a hospital or clinic placement, not just a high street pharmacy. I'd learn the software during my Saturday job. I'd also help my parents modernise the shop a bit, with online orders and delivery, to keep it going longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more able to cope. There's time to do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change the family plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The time lets me move toward clinical pharmacy before the robots take dispensing. Five years lets me move into clinical pharmacy before robots take over dispensing, which is where a lot of today's jobs are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the pharmacy to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask them to let staff train in clinical skills, like reviewing patients' medicines, and tell us honestly how many places they'll have. I'd ask for a written plan, not just chats at the counter.

say: I'd say five years is a **chance**, and we shouldn't waste it arguing.
I'd say families like mine need **loans and advice**.
think: I'd qualify in 2030, **a year before** AGI, into a changing job.
Robots in 2034 would probably take **dispensing**, so I'd want clinical work.
do: Finish the degree and aim for a **hospital or clinic** placement.
Help my parents add **online orders** and delivery to the shop.
feel: **Anxious**, but better able to cope, because there's time.
S3.quote: Five years lets me move into clinical pharmacy before robots take over dispensing, which is where a lot of today's jobs are.
fieldNote: The **five years** let her aim at clinical pharmacy before dispensing is automated.
Wants a **written plan** from employers, which fits her careful nature.
Links her own plan to **modernising** her parents' shop.

steps.text: Aim for a hospital clinical placement in my third year
Learn the pharmacy's dispensing software on Saturday shifts
Help my parents set up online orders and local delivery
Sit down with my parents every term to review shop sales

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a great gift, and sensible families will use it. I'd say don't rush in, learn what you can. And I'd say we should look after our neighbours who can't adapt, because that's what a community is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly calm. I'd have about six years as a pharmacist before AGI, enough to pay my loan, help my parents and perhaps own a share of a pharmacy. By 2039 the robots would be in my work, and I'd be in my late twenties and able to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, qualify, and work in a pharmacy that's open to clinical work. I'd save for my parents' retirement, since they've given me so much. And I'd probably marry in that time and want a home near family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. There's a bit of worry for the shop, but I'd feel like we can handle it as a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a decade give you and your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I would, because the job helps people directly, and that doesn't go out of fashion. Pharmacy helps people directly, and I'd still choose it with ten years' notice, because that part doesn't go out of fashion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still choose pharmacy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also help my parents sell or close the shop in a good way, if they wanted to stop. They've worked since they were twenty, and they should have a calm retirement.

say: I'd say ten years is a **great gift**, and sensible families will use it.
I'd say we should look after neighbours who **can't adapt**.
think: I'd have about **six years** as a pharmacist before AGI.
By 2039 I'd be in my late twenties and **able to move**.
do: Finish the degree and work in a pharmacy open to **clinical work**.
Marry and make a home **near family**.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a bit of worry for the shop.
S4.quote: Pharmacy helps people directly, and I'd still choose it with ten years' notice, because that part doesn't go out of fashion.
fieldNote: The **decade** lets her think about her parents' **retirement**, not just their survival.
Still **chooses** pharmacy because it helps people directly.
Community duty is a steady **theme** in her answers.

steps.text: Qualify as a pharmacist and work in a clinical pharmacy role
Save towards my parents' retirement from my first salary
Help my parents wind down the shop calmly when they choose

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My degree and my parents' shop would both be hit at once, and I'd have no time to prepare either. What would help is cheap loans for small shops, a clear plan from pharmacies about jobs, and people in the community looking out for each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm doing this for my family as much as for me. Whatever happens, I want to be the one who helps, not the one who needs help.

headlineQuote: I'm doing this for my family as much as for me.
portrait: Esther is a 19-year-old **pharmacy** student who works Saturdays at a high street pharmacy.
Her parents run a corner shop, and she does the till for them in the holidays.
She is traditional, faith-minded and uses AI now and then, but mostly trusts people and community.
She is **uneasy** when little changes, **alarmed** in the two-year world, and settled with ten years.
She plans to move to clinical pharmacy, help modernise the shop and look after her parents.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, where her degree and her parents' shop would both be hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small shops and a clear plan from pharmacies about jobs.
People in the **community** looking out for each other.
